name: Fatima Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day in your life now, and what your working life was like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I wake before dawn for prayer, then make tea and read the messages from my son Leo, who lives abroad. Mornings I reupholster chairs in the back room for customers who find me through the neighbourhood group. After lunch I walk to my daughter Yasmin's to see my granddaughters. I talk to an AI assistant every day, to translate Leo's long messages, draft quotes and find out how to fix a spring. I was an upholsterer for forty-one years in a furniture workshop on Canal Street, and I stopped at sixty-two after my husband Karim passed away.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does your faith or community give you in a normal week, and what's it like to be on your own now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I loved turning an old chair into something that looked new. The workshop was owned by a man who valued quality, until his sons took over and moved to cheap foam and staples. I couldn't do that kind of work, so I left. I'm a widow now, living alone in a rented flat, and my pension is basic. The chairs bring in a little, maybe 200 a month, and that's what lets me keep my head up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it with friends, family, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, it's a tool, and the people selling it are exaggerating. I'd tell my neighbours at the community centre that it's useful for little things, like forms and translation, but it won't change what makes a good life. I'd say that family and honest work still matter most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, privately, there's not much change. I already use the assistant every day, and it saves me time on quotes and instructions. What worries me is that I live alone on a basic pension. The rent is 590 and it goes up every year. If I fell ill, who'd help? My daughter would, but she's busy with her own children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the chairs and take a few more orders from the neighbourhood group. I'd ask the assistant to help me write better listings and photo captions, so more people find me. I'd keep my daily visit to Yasmin's. And I'd ask my landlord kindly about the rent, because we've known each other for ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels steady. I'm used to quiet. My faith gives me peace most of the time. But a little worry sits at the back, like a pebble in a shoe, about money and about being alone if I get ill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a pebble in a shoe. When did you last feel it most strongly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the rent rose by 50, I'd cut the weekly taxi, which I use for heavy fabric, and I'd shop at the market's last hour for cheaper food. I'd also take on two more chairs a week. I don't want to depend on my children. They have their own loads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you learned it to talk to Leo. What was the first thing you managed that surprised you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What's a bit different about me is that I'm not afraid of the technology. I learned to use the assistant because my son Leo is far away and I wanted to talk to him. It taught me that older people can learn if someone is patient. I'd say that to anyone who thinks we can't.

I'd say **family** and honest work still matter most.
think: Little changes for me, but I live alone on a basic pension with **rent** of 590 that rises each year.
If I fell ill, my daughter would help, but she's busy with her **own children**.
do: Take a few more **chair orders** through the neighbourhood group.
Ask the assistant to help write better **listings** and photo captions.
Ask my **landlord** kindly about the rent.
feel: It feels **steady**, with a little worry like a pebble in a shoe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it with friends, family, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and we should use it wisely. I'd tell my neighbours that families should talk to their young about work, because the young will be hit first. I'd say we should look after those who lose out, and the government should help with training and fair rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's mixed. The desk jobs will shrink, and my daughter Yasmin is a pharmacist, which has a lot of checking and paperwork the AI could do. I'd worry about her. But for my chairs, people want handmade things and want to know who made them, so I might do better. I'd just need to use the tools to reach customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the assistant to make a small online page for my upholstery, with before and after photos. I'd learn how to take good photos with the phone. I'd offer to teach a Thursday class at the community centre, 'Fix your own chair', for 10 a head. I'd sit with Yasmin and ask what her pharmacy plans to do. And I'd save 40 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels exciting and a bit sad. Exciting for what I can do, sad for those who don't have the help I do. I'd pray for the young and for our little community.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your daughter might be hit by the AI. What would you say to her that evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Yasmin's pharmacy used machines for checking, she'd still be needed to talk to patients, I think. People want a human, especially when they're sick. I'd say to her, be the one who talks and listens, not the one who counts pills. That's what the future needs, a kind face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the Thursday 'Fix your own chair' class look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also tell the young people at the centre, learn the tools and a real skill. You can have both. When I started, upholstery was hands only. Now I use my hands and the screen. The mix works. And if the sofa's springs are broken, no chatbot will fix them.

I'd say the government should help with **training** and fair rules.
think: Yasmin's pharmacy paperwork could be done by AI, which makes me **worry** for her.
People want **handmade** things, so my chairs might do better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it with friends, family, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, this is serious, and we should pray and prepare. Two years isn't long. I'd say it at the community centre and to my children: stay close, look after your parents, and keep your jobs while you can. I'd say the government has to make a plan fast, for everyone, not only for the rich.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm anxious, and a bit shaky. Yasmin's job and my son Leo's job abroad are both desk jobs, so they could both be at risk. If they lose them, who helps me? My pension is basic and the rent is 590. I'd have no cushion. I don't think of what I'd do, I think of what could happen to them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Yasmin and Leo and ask them to put money aside right now, even a little. I'd save every coin, 60 a month if I can by skipping the taxi and the market treats. I'd ask my landlord for a longer lease at the same rent. I'd get more chair orders, and I'd ask the community centre about its help for elders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like standing in a doorway with the wind pushing. I want to hold on to what I have. I'd pray more, and call Leo more often.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would two years be harder than longer for your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means my daughter's work changes first, her checking and counting. The hands-on work comes about three years later, so my chairs are safe a while. But I don't know if people will have money to buy chairs. That's what worries me, not the machine. A person who can't pay can't buy a chair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a longer lease do for you, in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Yasmin to consider living with me if she loses her job, although my flat is small. We'd share the rent and manage somehow. I'd rather share a small place than be alone in a big silence. I'd say it gently, so she doesn't feel like a burden.

I'd tell my children to **stay close** and keep their jobs while they can.

fieldNote: Her fear is **both children's** desk jobs, which are her safety net.
Offers to share her small flat with her daughter if needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it with friends, family, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent time. I'd say it's for families to talk and plan, and for the community to look out for its people. I'd tell the community centre to run classes for older people, and for young ones to learn trades. I'd say all this calmly, over tea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel more able. I'd be sixty-nine, and my daughters would be older and more settled. I'd have time to put by a bit, maybe a few hundred, and time to see what changes. The worry would still be the rent and my health, but not so sharp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save 40 a month. I'd grow my chair business with the online page, and teach the Thursday class more regularly. I'd ask Yasmin to learn the new tools at her pharmacy before they're forced on her. I'd also ask Leo to visit twice a year if he can. And I'd learn the new versions of the assistant as they come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a season changing. You feel it in the air. I'm a little nervous, but I like to plan. Planning calms me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would training a few neighbours to share your orders look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me do what two couldn't: build up a small cushion, train a few neighbours to do the work I do and share the orders, and help Yasmin plan. It also lets me think about moving closer to her, into a flat in her building, if the rent there is lower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to know before moving into Yasmin's building?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my granddaughters when they're older to learn what machines can't do well, like looking after people, working with their hands, listening. I'd say it in a story at bedtime, so it stays. A person is not a tool.

I'd tell the centre to run **classes** for older people and trades for the young.
think: I'd feel **more able**, with time to put by a few hundred.
The worry would still be **rent** and health, but less sharp.

feel: It feels like a **season changing**, and planning calms me.
S3.quote: A person is not a tool.
fieldNote: Five years brings **planning** and calm, with neighbours trained to share her orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it with friends, family, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd say, is a gift. I'd say use it to learn, to save, and to be kind. I'd say the community should plan together, and the young should take trades and professions that need a human touch. I'd say it plainly and then go back to my chair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel calm. I'd be seventy-four. My daughters will be established. I may not even see the worst of it. I'd think about what to pass on to my granddaughters, which is skills, faith and a sense of duty. The one practical worry is health and the cost of care, but with ten years I can save for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working on the chairs, save 30 a month and grow the online page. I'd run the community class twice a month. I'd learn what the assistant can do next, and teach others. And I'd spend more time with my granddaughters, because that is what matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a long, slow sunset. I'm peaceful. There's some sadness for the world changing, but also hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is the longest warning. What would you do differently from the other four?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I'd train an apprentice, maybe a young woman who needs work. I'd teach her the craft and how to use the tools, so she can run a small business of her own. That would be my legacy. With two years I'd have no time for that, only for worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach an apprentice first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Leo or Yasmin asked me what to do, I'd say, you have a decade. Learn the tools, save a little, and find work where people matter. And call your mother on Fridays. That I'd say in every scenario, and I mean it more than the rest.

say: I'd say use the decade to **learn**, to save and to be kind.
I'd say the young should take work that needs a **human touch**.
think: I'd feel **calm**, since my daughters will be established and I may not see the worst.
My one practical worry is **care costs**, which I can save for.

Run the community class **twice a month** and learn what the assistant does next.
feel: It feels like a **slow sunset**, peaceful with some sadness and hope.
S4.quote: With ten years I'd train an apprentice, maybe a young woman who needs work. I'd teach her the craft and how to use the tools

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because my children's desk jobs could go before they have time to prepare, and I'm on my own with a small pension. What would help is steady rent, a pension that keeps up with prices, classes for older people and a community that looks after its own. And people who take the time to explain, patiently.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that older women like me are not behind. We're often the ones keeping the family together. I'd ask whoever reads this to remember that a person with a sewing machine, a prayer mat and a tablet can be wise in all three. Don't assume we're old-fashioned. Ask us.

headlineQuote: A person with a sewing machine, a prayer mat and a tablet can be wise in all three.
portrait: Fatima is **64**, a retired upholsterer and widow who lives alone and uses an AI assistant every day.
Her **faith and family** run through every answer, and she wants to keep working and not depend on her children.
She earns a little from **chair repairs** and teaching, and sees AI as a tool, not a threat.
Her fear is for her children's **desk jobs** and her own rent on a basic pension.
biggestWorry: Two years worries her most, because her children's **desk jobs** could go before they can prepare.
whatWouldHelp: **Steady rent**, a price-linked pension, classes for older people and patient explanation.
